hero.title: How I Shipped What Millions of Nike Customers See First
hero.subtitle: Digital Content Manager (Contract) | Nike App and Nike.com

lede: From June to August 2026 I was a Digital Content Manager at Nike on a planned three-month contract. I published campaign content and app notifications to Nike.com and the Nike app, reaching as many as 20M customers per activation, verified delivery after each send, and co-developed the authoring reference the team now uses to onboard publishers. Every placement starts as a decision someone made upstream. Getting it live, correct, and on time was my job.

blocks.h: More Requests Than One Calendar Can Hold
p: Requests reach Nike's publishing team from marketing partners across the business, and one campaign can touch an app shopping surface, a landing page, a product grid, a notification, and the routing between them.

Some arrive incomplete: assets missing, timing that collides with work already scheduled, or a request the platform cannot support. With as many as 20 million people on the other end of one activation, delivery decides whether a campaign reaches anyone at all.

blocks.h: From Request to Live
p: I owned each placement from brief to verified delivery, and nothing was scheduled until it held up on a real phone. QA sign-off and legal review belonged to others; the build came back to me to schedule, and my part ended once delivery was confirmed.
Scroll through one placement to see which steps were mine.

steps.title: Intake the Brief
steps.d: A brief arrived from a marketing partner with the copy, imagery, links, and timing. I filled in what I could, and when something was missing or conflicting I went to the stakeholder who had the answer while the plan could still change.
checks: Timing clear of work already scheduled

steps.title: Build the Placement
steps.d: I built it in Nike's proprietary CMS: the module, the copy, the imagery, and the routing behind every tile and button.
checks: Every tile and button routes to a live destination
Alt text, captions, and heading structure in place

steps.title: Check It on a Real Device
steps.d: Before handing it off, I previewed it on a phone and on desktop, across breakpoints, in the app and on the web. Defects went to the development team with what I saw and where.
checks: Behaves the same in the app and on the web
Reads at a glance with the sound off
Copy and visuals hold to brand guidelines

steps.title: QA Sign-Off
steps.d: The build went to QA and came back signed off, or with fixes for me. I ran the same check on other publishers' builds, so I knew what QA would look for before I handed mine off.

steps.title: Legal Copy Review
steps.d: Claims and promotional copy cleared legal review before anything was released.

steps.title: Schedule the Release
steps.d: I scheduled it into a fixed publish window, coordinated with the operations, UX, and technical production teams. A claim that changed after sign-off went back through legal, and a changed link or image went back through the device check, before anything was released.
checks: No collision with placements already live

steps.title: Go Live and Verify
steps.d: After each send I confirmed the placement myself. Tests on headlines, featured products, and category entry points went into wrap briefs for campaign stakeholders, and those results belong to Nike.
checks: Live on Nike.com and in the app
Findings reported in the wrap brief

p: I joined with the World Cup already near its end and posted updates against live match results; Back to School needed athlete stories and full shopping surfaces; the U.S. Open needed its tennis shop live for the tournament. Smaller campaigns ran alongside these three.

I ran mine from request to live: placing the imagery and copy from the brief, building the placement, previewing it on a device, and routing it into its campaign.

p: Beyond single placements, I built complete shopping experiences: the hero, the category navigation, the product grid, and the routing that connects them. Where a surface carried SEO metadata and taxonomy tags, I set those in the CMS too.

blocks.h: Learn It, Then Teach It
p: I joined Nike's publishing team mid-season on a proprietary CMS I had never used, and kept my own notes as I learned it. With a teammate I co-developed the team's authoring reference, and before the contract ended as planned I trained the publishers staying on.

phases.d: Watched placements go through before building one.
Checked other publishers' builds against Figma, copy, alt text, and links, the fastest way to learn what breaks.
Took placements from brief to live on my own.
Co-developed the authoring reference and trained the publishers who stayed on.

blocks.topics: The reference covers platform constraints, accessibility standards, QA routing, scheduling rules, and how modules differ on mobile and desktop. The team adopted it as the onboarding guide for incoming publishers, which is the clearest sign it worked.

title: Christian's Work Portfolio with QAD Redzone

hero.title: Three Years Building Redzone's Brand and the Process Behind It
hero.subtitle: Digital Marketing & Web Content Specialist | QAD Redzone

lede: From June 2022 to August 2025 I was a Digital Marketing & Web Content Specialist at QAD Redzone, a connected workforce platform for plant floors. I joined as a new visual identity rolled out, working remotely on a marketing team of about three to five that grew to about fifteen. Over three years I built the intake process, 200+ SEO-optimized web and intranet pages, and the video, photography, and LinkedIn mix that put the people on the plant floor in front of the product, about half of it for customers and half for Redzone's own people.

blocks.h: A New Identity, a Small Team, No Intake Process
p: There was no intake process when I arrived. Requests came in with whatever the stakeholder had to hand, and the brand had a new identity to grow into.

Manufacturing software tends to look as cold as the factory floor it serves. Every competitor was very data heavy, with the person in the background. The product was wonderful, but the people running it on the floor were the story.

I owned the work end to end, from the first brainstorm to live: web content, organic social, paid media, video, and photography, with the landing pages behind them and the event leads tracked in Marketo, Salesforce, and 6sense.

blocks.h: From the Event Link to the Expo Floor
p: I owned creative and web requests from the first conversation to live. Review went back to the stakeholder (and on co-branded pages to the customer's team), and the work went out under my name.
Here are the five steps and which of them were mine.

steps.title: Lead the First Conversation
steps.d: Requests started with me in the room. I led the early brainstorms with stakeholders about what an event or campaign needed and what we had to work with. Even so, some arrived as literally the event link three weeks out, with nothing yet to catch what was missing.

steps.title: Build the Intake, Then Use It
steps.d: I built the intake form, the ticket, and the checklist in monday.com where none existed. After one launch package came in with too little time to do it well, the post-event surveys showed the real lead time was about two weeks, and that went into the form too.
checks: About two weeks of lead time

steps.title: Build It
steps.d: The landing page from scratch, the graphics, the video, or all three, and for the booth the jumbotron loop, built with the events team from campaign footage and animated UI. Stakeholders did not have to wait for creative; a request could come back in less than two hours.

steps.title: Stakeholders Review
steps.d: Internal stakeholders, and on co-branded pages the customer's team, reviewed over Slack and monday.com before anything went live.

steps.title: Live, and On to the Next One
steps.d: Live on the website, the intranet, the feed, or the booth. With intake catching what was missing, I could put out a fire instead of everything being a fire.

blocks.h: 200+ SEO-Optimized Pages and 33% More Traffic
p: Over three years I wrote and built 200+ SEO-optimized web and intranet pages, in the website's global CMS and in SharePoint on the intranet, from event landing pages made from scratch on short notice to co-branded industry pages with customer brands. By my own estimate a quarter of the website was written by me. I also built the launch package for the public 2023 Productivity Benchmark Report (landing page, gated download, social series, one-pager) and launched Redzone University in October 2023 (copy, graphics, brochures), tracking enrollment and reporting it up every month.

Traffic rose 33% year over year (56K to 75K sessions), target terms moved from page two into the top 3 results in 6 to 9 months, and lead generation rose 105% year over year. The paid campaigns I ran turned six-figure budgets into 1M+ ad interactions at twice the industry-average CTR. In 2024 my roughly fifteen colleagues voted me the Team Collaborator Award for that year's work, from the Learning campaign and the website to everything in between.

Beyond the pages, nurture and onboarding email lifted demo requests 10%, and a leave-a-review nurture campaign I ran fed Redzone's 2023 Top 100 listing on G2, where it reached #83 of 130,000 SaaS products with a 4.9 rating. The rest of the stack: WordPress, Adobe Experience Manager, monday.com, Marketo, HubSpot, Salesforce, 6sense, GA4, Google Tag Manager, Hotjar, Screaming Frog, and Figma.

blocks.h: From Fifth, to Fourth, to First Place in LinkedIn Engagement
p: When I joined, Redzone ranked fifth among its competitors on LinkedIn engagement. I tracked each post type every month and shifted the mix toward customer stories, humor, and short video, and the ranking moved to fourth, then to first.
LinkedIn engagement grew 7x (2% to 14%), and Reels and YouTube reach grew 3x (20K to 60K). Redzone was first among those competitors on LinkedIn engagement when I left in August 2025.

blocks.h: The Brand in Person: Trade Shows, Mailers, and Swag
p: Events were where the brand had to work in a room. A LinkedIn-post cutout gave attendees something to pose with and a tag to win an iPad, a shirt put an original character on people's backs, and for prospects a dimensional mailer built to look like an iPad box went out by their stage in the sales funnel.

blocks.h: Half the Work Faced the Company's Own People
p: About half of what I made was for Redzone's own people. I built and maintained my sections of the SharePoint intranet: the onboarding, training, and policy material I produced. The monthly work-anniversary posts ran from May 2024 to July 2025, the volunteer days and GivingTuesday drives got their promotion from the same desk, and I taught recurring internal sessions on social and personal branding.

title: Christian's Work Portfolio with SOLV Energy

hero.title: How I Modernized SOLV Energy's Web Presence and Built Power Apps That Streamlined Internal Workflows
hero.subtitle: Internal Tools & External Web for SOLV Energy

lede: SOLV Energy is a lifecycle partner for utility-scale solar, storage and energy infrastructure across the United States, with more than 20 GW of solar and storage under management and a listing on Nasdaq (MWH). A company building and announcing at that scale needs a digital presence that keeps up. This case study covers how I supported and built that presence across web, internal tools, graphic design and video.

blocks.h: THE PROBLEM
p: A renewable energy company has a harder communications job than most. SOLV Energy talks to investors, customers, prospective hires, craft workers, community partners and thousands of employees in offices and on jobsites across the country, and each group needs different proof points, formats and channels. Communications systems hadn't kept pace with that growth. The website needed steady, accurate updates as projects, leadership news and milestones landed. Internal teams needed a faster way to share approved content with their own networks. The visuals had to keep up with a project pipeline running in dozens of states at once.

blocks.h: THE SOLUTION
p: I handled the day-to-day work behind all of it: a continuously updated external website, internal tools that turned approved content into posts employees could share, graphic design at the pace project announcements demanded, and video that showed the work on the ground. I built each piece so it could grow with the company.

blocks.h: Owning the Web Presence and Internal Tooling of a Public Energy Infrastructure Company
p: A public company moves fast, and its website has to keep up. I maintained solvenergy.com in WordPress, publishing project announcements, leadership additions, earnings news and partnership wins as they landed. Updates often went live within hours of internal approval, with formatting, imagery and SEO checked before publish.

I also built and launched an Employee Advocacy platform in Power Apps. It gives SOLV Energy teammates one place to find pre-approved social content to share with their own networks, replacing a manual, email-based workflow. Employees can browse, preview and share posts to LinkedIn in seconds.
The site stayed current, and employees became a real channel for visibility and recruiting.

gallery.title: SOLV Energy Homepage Hero Walkthrough
gallery.desc:
This is the front door of solvenergy.com: a wide aerial of a solar field, the SOLV mark, and a hero line that sums up the company in four words, Powering Progress with Proven Execution. I kept the site current as project, leadership, and earnings news landed.
Updates often went live within hours of internal approval, with formatting, imagery, and SEO handled before publish so the homepage always reflected where the company actually was.
gallery.cap: I kept solvenergy.com current as project, leadership and earnings news landed.

gallery.title: Employee Advocacy Power App in Action
gallery.desc:
Sharing approved content used to mean digging through emails. I built this Employee Advocacy platform in Power Apps so SOLV Energy teammates have one place to find pre-approved posts, sorted by tags like Impact, Mission, and Project Spotlight.
Each card previews the post before sharing, and employees can push it straight to their LinkedIn in seconds. The result turned a manual workflow into a self-serve experience that helps with visibility and recruiting.
gallery.cap: I built this Power Apps platform for sharing approved posts to LinkedIn.

gallery.title: Publishing a News Article Behind the Scenes
gallery.desc:
Here's a look at the publishing side of the job: an article entry with its title, one-sentence extract, background image, and subject and media categories, shown next to a live preview of the SOLV Energy news page.
Every announcement went through this kind of setup before going live. I checked formatting, imagery, and categorization in the preview so each story looked right the moment it published.
gallery.cap: How I set up and checked each news article before it went live.

gallery.title: Design, Build, Operate, Optimize Services Page
gallery.desc:
A scroll through one of solvenergy.com's interior pages, opening on crews in hard hats at work in the field and the headline Design. Build. Operate. Optimize. It explains SOLV Energy's end-to-end services for solar, battery storage, and high-voltage infrastructure.
I kept pages like this accurate and current as the company grew, so customers and investors landing deeper in the site found the same polish as the homepage.
gallery.cap: One of the interior pages I kept accurate as the company grew.

blocks.h: Designing at the Speed of a Public Company's News Cycle
p: When SOLV Energy goes public, breaks ground or sends an executive to a conference, the visuals for that moment have to be ready fast, sometimes the same day. I produced ongoing graphic design across speaker session cards, kudos and recognition posts, project announcements and case study teasers, working within SOLV Energy's visual system and extending it over time.

I kept compositions clean, built palettes on SOLV Energy's signature colors and set headlines so each graphic still read at thumbnail size in a social feed. Assets shipped quickly and still held up for investors and customers.

gallery.title: RE+ 2025 Event and Speaking Session Graphics
gallery.desc:
For RE+ in Las Vegas, I made a pair of graphics: a bold blue announcement for the event and a darker companion piece listing SOLV Energy's two speaking sessions with Eric Butticaz, Director of Apprenticeship, including times and rooms.
The Venetian skyline and SOLV's sunburst mark tie the two together, while the lime accents and clear type keep the session details easy to read at thumbnail size on social.
gallery.cap: I made the event announcement and speaking session graphics for RE+ in Las Vegas.

gallery.title: Conference Speaker Card and Kudos Post
gallery.desc:
These two cover both sides of SOLV Energy's event presence. On the left, a speaking session card for CFO Chad Plotkin at the 38th Annual ROTH Conference. On the right, a kudos post recognizing Kate for representing the company at the 2026 IECA Annual Conference & Expo.
Both are built on the brand's signature blues and sunburst motif, with a headline hierarchy that stays readable even as a small social thumbnail.
gallery.cap: A speaker card for CFO Chad Plotkin and a kudos post, both designed by me.

gallery.title: Announcement and Case Study Teaser Graphics
gallery.desc:
Not every post needs a face. The left graphic is an "In Case You Missed It" announcement about SOLV Energy's O&M scale and largest single-site agreement, set over a field photo of solar panels and wildflowers.
The right is a case study teaser that opens with a question about underperforming sites. I let the white space and the sunburst frame do the work, ending with a simple prompt to read the case study.
gallery.cap: An announcement and a case study teaser I designed.

blocks.h: Bringing Field Stories and Project Milestones to Life Through Video
p: Video is how SOLV Energy shows its work to people who will never visit a jobsite. I helped concept, script and produce social videos and internal content for project milestones, customer testimonials and culture moments, and let the people doing the work speak for themselves.
Editing stayed minimal: on-site footage, a light brand overlay and pacing tuned for LinkedIn and for longer internal pieces.

A vertical social video that opens on a sweeping aerial of a SOLV Energy project under construction, with crews, trucks, and structures spread across the site. It's part of the short-form work I helped concept, script, and produce for project milestones and culture moments.
Editing stayed minimal so the work on the ground carried the story, with light branding and pacing tuned for social feeds.

Sometimes the best move is to let leadership talk. In this piece, CEO George Hershman speaks directly to camera in a relaxed interview setting about SOLV Energy and its work.
I kept the edit simple and the speaker central, matching the approach I used across SOLV's video content: let the people behind the company speak for themselves, with branding that supports the message instead of competing with it.

This vertical video gives a site overview of the Misae Solar project, starting with a drone shot over rows of panels stretching toward the horizon. It was one of several pieces I helped produce to show audiences what SOLV Energy's projects look like up close.
I paired on-site footage with light brand overlays and kept the pacing quick enough for LinkedIn while still giving the scale of the site room to land.

title: Christian's Work Portfolio with Cohesity

hero.title: How I Led Employee Advocacy for 3,000 Advocates and Cross-Channel Design at Cohesity
hero.subtitle: Employee Advocacy and Integrated Creative for an AI-Powered Data Security Leader

lede: Cohesity is a leader in AI-powered data security and management, trusted by 70% of the Global 500 across 140+ countries. Its brand and content needed to feel as human as the people behind it. This case study covers how I helped run Cohesity's Champions employee advocacy program and designed creative across PR, blogs, newsletters and global events.

blocks.h: THE PROBLEM
p: Enterprise cybersecurity content tends to be dense, technical and written for boardrooms more than for the people who share it, read it and deal with the threats it covers. Cohesity had strong product news, deep customer stories and real industry credibility, but its social voice and visuals blended in with the rest of enterprise software. Employees weren't sharing content they didn't connect with, and the brand was missing chances to reach both its own advocates and outside audiences.

blocks.h: THE SOLUTION
p: I wrote a new brand voice for the Champions employee advocacy program, closer to Duolingo and Figma on social than to corporate LinkedIn, and ran a daily content engine that gave 3,000 advocates posts they wanted to share. Alongside the advocacy work, I led original design for PR campaigns, blog hero graphics, newsletters and global event activations.

blocks.h: Reframing Cohesity's Voice for an Employee Advocacy Program That Actually Got Shared
p: I rebuilt the Employee Advocacy program from the ground up and ran its daily content for 3,000 advocate seats worldwide, across a company of 7,000 employees. Beyond writing the core posts, I led the program's redesign, ran internal competitions, expanded it into international markets and connected advocacy work across several departments. I also headed an executive advocacy program, writing and editing posts myself for the Chief Product Officer and the Chief Financial Officer. Employee posts became one of the company's strongest social channels.

gallery.title: Champions Advocacy Hub Trending Posts Feed
gallery.desc:
This is where Cohesity's Champions found content to share each day. The Trending Posts view shows the week's most active posts, from the HPE alliance to the agentic support portal, with a live feed of colleagues sharing alongside.
I wrote the posts that filled this feed in a voice closer to Duolingo and Figma social than corporate LinkedIn, so 3,000 advocates actually wanted to post them. Leaderboards and challenges kept the energy up.
gallery.cap: I wrote the posts that filled this feed for 3,000 advocates.

gallery.title: The Empire Strikes Backups Champions Newsletter
gallery.desc:
A Star Wars nod for a data security company was too good to pass up. The Empire Strikes Backups newsletter opens with a glowing green title over a starfield, followed by a Top Content to Share ticker and story cards with one-click Share buttons.
I designed it to make sharing feel like a game for Champions, pulling the week's best posts into a single scroll so advocates could share in seconds without hunting for links.
gallery.cap: A Star Wars nod I designed for the Champions newsletter.

blocks.h: Pushing Brand Voice and Visuals Through Creative Holiday Content
p: Beyond employee advocacy, I supported the creative team on Cohesity's most visible moments: partnership campaigns with Google Cloud, AWS, NVIDIA, Hewlett-Packard and Microsoft, blog hero graphics for executive thought leadership, creative for the weekly Security Spotlight and Empire Strikes Backups newsletters, and event activations. The visuals had to look as modern as consumer design and still carry credibility in enterprise cybersecurity.

gallery.title: Webinar, Hiring, and NVIDIA GTC Social Graphics
gallery.desc:
Three posts, three different jobs: a webinar promo on ransomware gang behavior, a bold pink We're Hiring card for a role in São Paulo, and an event graphic for Cohesity at NVIDIA GTC 2026.
Each one leans on Cohesity's green and magenta palette and tight condensed type, so they read like a set while handling very different messages. The goal was consumer-grade energy that still felt credible in enterprise security.
gallery.cap: A webinar promo, a hiring card and an NVIDIA GTC graphic I designed.

gallery.title: Google Cloud Next, Blog Hero, and Newsletter Creative
gallery.desc:
A mix from Cohesity's busiest channels: a booth promo for Google Cloud Next 26 in Las Vegas, a blog hero announcing that the future of support is here and it's agentic, and a punchy Your backups are next. graphic.
I kept each piece simple and direct, letting the bright green and big type carry the message so it held up across events, blogs, and weekly Security Spotlight newsletter creative.
